Eggs of the Black fantail, Rhipidura atra, incubated at 32 °C [T = 32 °C] hatch after an average of 16 days [ab = 16 days], a developmental period comparable to that of the related antbird Willisornis poecilinotus. The freshly laid eggs, measuring approximately 18 mm in length and 13.8 mm in width, produce neonates with an initial wet weight of only 1.8 grams [Ww0 = 1.8 grams], a value derived from the standard volumetric formula for ellipsoid bird eggs. This remarkably small hatchling mass underscores the extreme altriciality of the young, which are entirely dependent on parental provisioning from the moment of hatching. Females invest heavily in the single nest, and the hatchlings display no thermoregulatory capability for the first several days post-emergence, requiring constant brooding by the attending adult to maintain body temperature. The size of the egg relative to the adult female is modest, which is consistent with patterns observed in other small-bodied monarch flycatchers of the Australo-Pacific region.

Under the standard thermal conditions typical of the active metabolic period for this species, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the nestling period proceeds through a series of well-defined developmental milestones. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight sufficient to leave the nest, occurs at 18 days after hatching [tx = 18 days after hatching], a timing that has been documented in detailed observational studies of the species at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Shortly thereafter, the attainment of sexual maturity is observed at 54 days after hatching [tp = 54 days after hatching], a remarkably swift progression to reproductive competence for a passerine of this body size at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid maturation likely reflects an adaptive response to the high levels of nest predation and adult mortality that characterize life in the montane forests of New Guinea. The fledgling cohort disperses from the natal territory within a few days of achieving independence, and the young birds begin to explore foraging microhabitats similar to those used by the adults.

Adult females of the Black fantail attain a maximum body mass of 12.2 grams [Wwi = 12.2 grams], a value that falls comfortably within the typical range of 11 to 12 grams reported for the species across its elevational distribution. This ultimate wet weight is achieved only after the completion of skeletal growth and the full development of flight musculature, which occurs several weeks after the onset of independent feeding. Body mass remains relatively stable throughout the adult life stage, with only minor fluctuations associated with reproductive events such as egg laying and the energetically demanding period of nestling provisioning. Field measurements of captured individuals indicate that males are slightly lighter on average, though the difference is rarely statistically significant and tends to be obscured by the considerable individual variation present within any given population. The species occupies a relatively narrow body mass range among the monarch flycatchers, which is consistent with its insectivorous diet and active foraging mode.

The maximum lifespan recorded for this species, based on a long-term mark-recapture study conducted under natural conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 3139 days [am = approximately 3139 days], which equates to roughly 8.6 years. This longevity is relatively high for a tropical passerine of its size and is thought to be facilitated by the low extrinsic mortality rates typical of montane forest environments, where predator densities are comparatively low. Older individuals often show signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch sizes and lower fledging success in the final year of life. Population viability models suggest that this extended adult lifespan is critical for offsetting the high rates of egg and nestling mortality that characterize the early stages of the life cycle. The oldest confirmed individual was a female first captured as an adult and subsequently recaptured over eight consecutive field seasons, providing robust data on the species' actuarial schedule.

The maximum reproductive rate, realized under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], involves the production of a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch] and approximately one clutch each year [F_R_i = approximately one clutch each year]. This extremely low reproductive output is among the most striking features of the species' life history and is likely a consequence of the intense parental investment required to rear a single nestling to independence in a resource-limited environment. The age at first successful brood is 438 days since birth [tR = 438 days since birth], meaning that young females typically do not breed until their second calendar year at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Furthermore, basal metabolic rate measurements obtained through flow-through respirometry at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] reveal a maximum resting oxygen consumption of 55.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 55.5 milliliters per hour], a value that reflects the high energetic demands of thermoregulation and foraging activity in this small-bodied insectivore.
